0.body: This repository implements Bazel rules for Python and is designed to be a drop-in replacement for the existing rules_python where uses of @rules_python//python:defs.bzl can be replaced with @rules_venv//python:defs.bzl.
0.title: rules_venv

1.body: While rules_python has fantastic toolchain infrastructure which this repo relies on, rules_python ultimately suffers from a few issues which this repo aims to solve: Use of PYTHONPATH to construct the python environment leads to operating system limitations. Some details on MAX_ARG_STRLEN and ARG_MAX can be found here: https://unix.stackexchange.com/a/120842 Slow startup on windows systems that do not support symlinks. rules_python creates zipapps on systems that do not support runfiles. For large projects, this can lead to large (~500MB+) zip files being constantly compressed and uncompressed to run simple actions which is a lot more expensive than systems which support runfiles.
1.title: Improvements over rules_python

31.body: Bazel rules for generating usable virtualenv from Bazel targets.
31.title: Global Venv

32.body: A venv can be created by invoking the following command bazel run @rules_venv//python/global_venv From here a venv will likely be available at .venv within your workspace that can be activated for improved IDE support.
32.title: Usage

33.body:
By default, a bazel-pyrightconfig.json is generated with extraPaths pointing to each Bazel output directory that contains generated Python sources. To use it, add an extends field to your pyrightconfig.json: { "extends": "bazel-pyrightconfig.json"
} Important: Do not define extraPaths in your own pyrightconfig.json. Pyright's extends replaces array fields rather than merging them, so any extraPaths in the child config will override the generated values.
33.title: Pyright / Pylance

34.body:
Ruff classifies imports as first-party by checking whether the imported module can be resolved under its src directories. Generated sources (.pyi stubs, .so extensions) only exist under bazel-out, so ruff needs those directories in src: # .ruff.toml
src = [".", "bazel-out/k8-*/bin"] For standalone isort: # .isort.cfg
[isort]
src_paths = .,bazel-out/k8-*/bin The glob k8-* covers all Bazel configurations (k8-fastbuild, k8-opt, k8-dbg).
34.title: Ruff / isort

35.body:
By default, py_global_venv auto-discovers console_scripts entrypoints from pip packages (via importlib.metadata) and generates executable scripts in the venv's bin/ directory. Pre-built binaries shipped via wheel data scripts (e.g. ruff) are also symlinked into the venv. This allows IDEs to find tools like black, ruff, or mypy inside the venv. Additional entrypoints can be specified manually: py_global_venv( name = "global_venv", entrypoints = { "my_tool": "my.module:cli", },
) Auto-discovery can be disabled with gen_entrypoints = False.
35.title: Entrypoints

38.body:
load("@rules_venv//python/global_venv:defs.bzl", "py_global_venv") py_global_venv(*, name, gen_pyrightconfig, gen_entrypoints, entrypoints, build_srcs, **kwargs) Define a "global venv" executable. When gen_pyrightconfig is enabled (the default), running this target writes a bazel-pyrightconfig.json at the workspace root containing extraPaths that point into bazel-bin. This lets Pyright/Pylance resolve generated Python sources that live outside the source tree. To use it, add an extends field to your pyrightconfig.json:: { "extends": "bazel-pyrightconfig.json", ...
} Important: Do not define extraPaths in your own pyrightconfig.json when using extends. Pyright's extends replaces array fields rather than merging them, so any extraPaths in the child config will override the generated values from bazel-pyrightconfig.json. When targets use configuration transitions (e.g. py_cc_extension building with compilation_mode = "opt"), generated files may live in directories like bazel-out/k8-opt/bin instead of bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/bin. The generated bazel-pyrightconfig.json includes all observed output directories automatically. For ruff or isort to correctly classify first-party imports that include generated sources, add the Bazel output directories to the src setting:: # .ruff.toml
src = [".", "bazel-out/k8-*/bin"] For standalone isort :: # .isort.cfg
[isort]
src_paths = .,bazel-out/k8-*/bin This allows ruff/isort to find generated .pyi stubs and .so extensions when determining whether an import is first-party or third-party. When gen_entrypoints is enabled (the default), running this target will auto-discover console_scripts entrypoints from pip packages via importlib.metadata and generate executable scripts in the venv's bin/ directory. Pre-built binaries shipped via wheel data scripts (e.g. ruff) are also symlinked into the venv. This allows IDEs to find tools like black, ruff, or mypy inside the venv. Additional entrypoints can be specified manually via entrypoints. PARAMETERS Name Description Default Value name The name of the target none gen_pyrightconfig Generate a bazel-pyrightconfig.json to support indexing Bazel generated files. True gen_entrypoints Auto-discover console_scripts entrypoints from pip packages and generate executable scripts in the venv bin/ directory. True entrypoints A mapping of script names to module specs (e.g. {"black": "black:patched_main"}). These are always rendered regardless of gen_entrypoints. When gen_entrypoints is also enabled, manual entries take precedence over auto-discovered ones. {} build_srcs Build all python sources to ensure they're available for loading. False kwargs Additional keyword arguments for the py_binary. none
38.title: py_global_venv

4.body: By default each launch of a py_binary or py_test builds its venv in a temporary directory that is deleted on exit, so sys.executable is only valid while the process runs. When this variable is set, the venv is instead built at $RULES_VENV_EXTRACT_ROOT/<repo>/<package>/<name>.venv (with _main for the main repository) and, on platforms without runfiles support, the rendered runfiles tree beside it as <name>.runfiles. Both are left in place and reused by later launches of the same target unless the interpreter, import paths, or runfiles collection have changed. Cleaning up the root is the responsibility of the caller. A relative path is resolved against the working directory.
4.title: RULES_VENV_EXTRACT_ROOT

60.body: load("@rules_venv//python/mypy:defs.bzl", "py_mypy_toolchain") py_mypy_toolchain(name, config, mypy) A toolchain for the mypy formatter rules. ATTRIBUTES Name Description Type Mandatory Default name A unique name for this target. Name required config The config file (mypy.ini) containing mypy settings.Settings and mypy version together decide what a cache entry means, so they are named in one place. The default tracks the @rules_venv//python/mypy:config flag, which is how a workspace that has not defined its own toolchain chooses a config file. Label optional "@rules_venv//python/mypy:config" mypy The mypy py_library to use with the rules.Must be mypy 2.0 or newer. These rules analyze a dependency once and share the result with everything that imports it, which rests on mypy checking function bodies only where the errors are wanted -- a split mypy grew in 2.0. An older release is refused rather than tolerated, since on a large dependency the difference is seconds against half an hour. Label required

61.body: load("@rules_venv//python/mypy:defs.bzl", "py_mypy_aspect") py_mypy_aspect() An aspect for running mypy on targets with Python sources. Every Python target the aspect reaches publishes a PyMypyCacheInfo , including the ones it does not check. Targets that opt out with a no_mypy tag, and third-party packages, are analyzed but not reported on. It travels every attribute rather than deps alone, since a rule is free to build its PyInfo from any of them. A library reached through a toolchain cannot be followed that way at all, so a target whose Python none of its attributes accounts for caches everything it publishes as one unit. That needs nothing of the rule but the PyInfo it already returns, so a toolchain defined outside this repository gets the same treatment without doing anything. ASPECT ATTRIBUTES ATTRIBUTES
61.title: py_mypy_aspect

87.body: Build Python into a self-contained WebAssembly module: CPython and the sources of py_library targets, callable from any WebAssembly runtime, with no Python interpreter on the host. The module is CPython built for wasm32-wasi and linked with an in-module implementation of the WASI functions it would otherwise import, so that it imports nothing and a runtime that provides no host functions at all can instantiate it. Inside it run the unmodified sources of the py_library targets named by deps, served by an importer over a bundle linked into the module, together with the standard library as bytecode. By default the interpreter is started and the entry module imported at build time, with Wizer, and the memory snapshot becomes the module, so a call does not pay for start-up.
87.title: py_wasm_module

88.body: Nothing beyond depending on rules_venv and registering, with rules_python, a hermetic Python toolchain of a version the rule supports: 3.13, 3.14, and 3.15 once rules_python maps it to a final release. Modules are built with a py_wasm_toolchain, and rules_venv registers one for each such version and each Linux and macOS host (x86_64 and arm64), made of the wasm32-wasi build of that CPython release from periareon/cpython-wasi-build , the wasi-sdk release that built it and Wizer, which its py_wasm extension fetches when a module is first built. The CPython comes in variants, the default being the fastest under Bazel's runtime; see "The CPython" below. A compiler or CPython of one's own is another py_wasm_toolchain; see "Toolchains" below.
88.title: Setup

89.body: A hermetic rules_python toolchain of the module's python_version, a final release. Its C headers compile the module's host code and its interpreter produces the bytecode for the one in the module, so the two must be the same X.Y and a pre-release, whose bytecode and ABI may differ, is refused; the rule fails on either, and the build tools check again when they run. A py_wasm_toolchain for that version on the host, and Wizer when preinitialize is on. The rule fails when preinitialize has no Wizer. Code that runs on CPython for WASI: a source the embedded interpreter cannot import fails at build time with its traceback when preinitialize is on, else at the first call.
89.title: Requirements

) ATTRIBUTES Name Description Type Mandatory Default name A unique name for this target. Name required deps Other python targets to link to the current target. List of labels optional [] srcs The list of source (.py) files that are processed to create the target. List of labels optional [] data Files needed by this rule at runtime. May list file or rule targets. Generally allows any target. List of labels optional [] env Dictionary of strings; values are subject to $(location) and "Make variable" substitution. Dictionary: String -> String optional {} imports List of import directories to be added to the PYTHONPATH. 90.title: Use

91.body:
The module exports its memory as memory, an allocator, and one function per entry of exports: allocate(size: u32, align: u32) -> u32 the address of `size` bytes
<export>(input: u32, input_len: u32, out_ptr: u32, out_len: u32) -> u32 the return code A host writes the input into memory it obtained from allocate, calls the export with the addresses of two more words to receive the output's address and length, and reads the output back from memory. The return code is 0, or the code the function returned with (bytes, code), or 2 when it raised, in which case the output holds the traceback and what was written to standard error. With Python's wasmtime package: import wasmtime store = wasmtime.Store(wasmtime.Engine())
module = wasmtime.Module.from_file(store.engine, "my_rules.wasm")
exports = wasmtime.Instance(store, module, []).exports(store)
memory = exports["memory"] payload = json.dumps(request).encode("utf-8")
input_ptr = exports["allocate"](store, len(payload), 1)
memory.write(store, payload, input_ptr)
out = exports["allocate"](store, 8, 4)
code = exports["run"](store, input_ptr, len(payload), out, out + 4)
out_ptr = int.from_bytes(memory.read(store, out, out + 4), "little")
out_len = int.from_bytes(memory.read(store, out + 4, out + 8), "little")
output = bytes(memory.read(store, out_ptr, out_ptr + out_len)) A call changes the instance's memory, and instances are independent, so a host that wants every call to be a function of its input alone instantiates the module per call. Any runtime that can instantiate a module without imports and call exports with integer arguments can be the host; examples/py_wasm_module in the rules_venv repository has a Bazel repository rule calling a module with repository_ctx.execute_wasm this way.
91.title: Calling the module

92.body: Nothing outside the module: no files, network, clock or processes. Standard output and error are captured inside the module; the error stream of a failed call is returned with the traceback. A program that needs the outside world receives what it needs in its input and describes what it wants done in its output, in rounds if need be. Bytes cross the boundary unchanged in both directions.
92.breadcrumbs: Extensions » wasm » What a call can do
92.title: What a call can do

93.body: The CPython in a module is a release built for wasm32-wasi by periareon/cpython-wasi-build , pinned by version and hash in python/wasm/private/versions.bzl together with the wasi-sdk release that built it. Of that build the rule uses pyconfig.h, libpython and the libraries of the modules compiled into it, and its standard library as source; the public headers are the rules_python toolchain's, and the bytecode is produced at build time by that toolchain's interpreter, which is why the two must be the same version. Each version comes in variants that differ in how the interpreter is compiled, because the runtime decides which build is fast. Bazel runs a module with Chicory, which compiles each wasm function to one JVM method and interprets, silently, any function too large for one; CPython's evaluation loop is such a function in its normal build, and a Python-heavy call then spends most of its time in that interpreter (a solver call measured 88 s against 2.5 s). So: stock: CPython's own WASI build, as brettcannon/cpython-wasi-build publishes it; the fastest under wasmtime. small-eval: built for size with the evaluation loop kept under the limit, so that Chicory compiles everything; about ten times faster there. trampoline (3.14 and newer): the tail-calling interpreter turned into a call-threaded one, with no function anywhere near the limit; the fastest under Chicory, about twice as slow as stock under wasmtime. The default is the fastest under Chicory: trampoline for 3.14, small-eval for 3.13, stock where it is the only build. Modules run elsewhere pick another with the //python/wasm:cpython_variant flag, in .bazelrc or on the command line; it applies to every version at once, and a version without the variant asked for fails saying which it has: build --@rules_venv//python/wasm:cpython_variant=stock
93.title: The CPython

94.body: A module is built with a py_wasm_toolchain: the clang of a wasi-sdk, a CPython built for wasm32-wasi (libpython, the libraries of its modules, its pyconfig.h and its standard library), the flags that CPython links with, and Wizer. Two of rules_python's toolchains take part as well, resolved for the same Python version: its C toolchain, for the headers, and its exec tools toolchain, for the interpreter that produces the module's bytecode.
94.title: Toolchains

95.body: rules_venv registers a toolchain for every Python version pinned in python/wasm/private/versions.bzl that the resolved rules_python maps to a final release, 3.13 and 3.14 today, for Linux and macOS on x86_64 and arm64. Its py_wasm extension declares the archives and writes the toolchains into the repository @rules_venv_py_wasm_toolchains. Nothing is fetched until a module is built, and then only what the resolved toolchain needs. Each toolchain is gated on rules_python's is_python_X.Y, which a module's python_version sets, so the embedded CPython always matches the Python toolchain the module is built with; a version rules_python maps to a pre-release is left out, and the rule refuses one, since its bytecode and ABI may differ from the release's.
95.title: The defaults

96.body: Declare a py_wasm_toolchain and a toolchain gated on is_python_X.Y, as in the documentation of py_wasm_toolchain, and register it with register_toolchains in MODULE.bazel or with --extra_toolchains. A root module's toolchains take precedence over rules_venv's, which remain as the fallback for other versions and hosts. Reasons to: a CPython built differently, with other configure options or patches; a version or host rules_venv has no build for; a policy of building from source; or a newer wasi-sdk, which must be the release that built the CPython so that their wasi-libc agree. linkopts and stdlib of the toolchain cover smaller adjustments: what the CPython links against, and which standard library modules go into a module.
96.breadcrumbs: Extensions » wasm » One of your own
96.title: One of your own

97.body:
To keep a default toolchain but swap one of its parts, point the extension's repository for it elsewhere. In MODULE.bazel: py_wasm = use_extension("@rules_venv//python/wasm:extensions.bzl", "py_wasm")
override_repo(py_wasm, rules_venv_py_wasm_cpython_3_14_trampoline = "my_cpython_wasi") or, for a checkout on disk, --override_repository=rules_venv++py_wasm+rules_venv_py_wasm_cpython_3_14_trampoline=<directory>. The repositories are rules_venv_py_wasm_cpython_<X_Y>_<variant> (the build tree: libpython3.X.a, pyconfig.h, Modules/**/*.a; one per variant of the version, the flag choosing among them), ..._cpython_<X_Y>_<variant>_stdlib (lib/python3.X/**/*.py), rules_venv_py_wasm_wasi_sdk_<release>_<host> and rules_venv_py_wasm_wizer_<host>; a replacement provides the same targets as the BUILD files in extensions.bzl.
97.title: Replacing one archive

99.body: load("@rules_venv//python/wasm:defs.bzl", "py_wasm_module") py_wasm_module(name, deps, entry, exports, initial_memory, preinitialize, python_version, stack_size, strip) Build a self-contained WebAssembly module embedding CPython and Python sources. The output, <name>.wasm, imports nothing and exports memory, allocate and one function per entry of exports; the module documentation of defs.bzl gives the calling convention. Each export calls the function of the same name in the entry module with the call's input as bytes and returns what it returns: bytes, or (bytes, code) to set the return code. An exception becomes return code 2 with the traceback in the output. The module holds the sources of deps as a venv would import them, the standard library as bytecode, and, by default, a snapshot of the interpreter taken after the entry module was imported, so that a call does not pay for start-up. The CPython is the one of python_version, which also selects the rules_python toolchain the module is built with. See the module documentation of defs.bzl and py_wasm_toolchain. ATTRIBUTES Name Description Type Mandatory Default name A unique name for this target. Name required deps The Python libraries the entry module imports, bundled with their transitive dependencies. List of labels optional [] entry The dotted name of the module holding the exported functions, e.g. my_rules.wasm.entry. String required exports The functions of entry to export, each under its own name. List of strings required initial_memory The initial size of the module's memory, in bytes. It grows as needed, up to any limit the runtime imposes. Integer optional 67108864 preinitialize Snapshot the interpreter after importing entry with Wizer, so a call starts from there. Without it every call starts the interpreter, which can take seconds under an interpreting runtime. Boolean optional True python_version The Python version to build for, X.Y: the module embeds that CPython and is built with that rules_python toolchain, which must be registered. Unset, the build's current Python version, which must have a py_wasm_toolchain; see "Toolchains" in the module documentation of defs.bzl. String optional "" stack_size The size of the C stack, in bytes. Integer optional 8388608 strip Strip the name section and other debug information from the module. Boolean optional True
99.title: py_wasm_module
